endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Document the current tool in use, its limitations, and whether it meets the key capabilities needed: searchable and accessible to governance stakeholders, version-controlled

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether auditing the AI inventory on a set cadence and reconciling it against other organizational records finds missing or stale entries, and no study documents how often such entries occur. The recommendation rests on one framework endorsement from CHAI, which calls for a searchable, accessible, version-controlled inventory tool but does not specify an audit cadence or reconciliation method.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single endorsement reflects expert consensus from a framework, which may guide practice but does not show effect.

No supplied study measures how often shadow AI tools or outdated inventory entries occur, or whether an unlisted tool has led to patient harm. Without such data, the size of the hazard and the share of errors that a periodic audit would catch remain unknown.

The CHAI playbook rates inventory documentation as a must and lists searchability, stakeholder access, and version control as required capabilities. Its quoted language addresses the inventory tool itself. It does not state how often audits should occur or which organizational records, such as procurement or IT asset lists, should be used for reconciliation.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems with and without scheduled inventory reconciliation, measuring the number of unlisted or outdated AI tools found, the staff time each audit requires, and whether audit frequency changes the rate of discovery. Baseline studies that estimate how many deployed AI tools are missing from inventories would also establish the size of the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may operate with fewer governance staff, and whether a scheduled audit is feasible or useful in those settings has not been examined.
